title: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
summary: How stackless coroutines make waiting cheap: Rust futures as lazy state machines, poll and wakers wired to epoll, Tokio's work-stealing scheduler, and the cooperative scheduling rules that bite in production.
outcomes: Explain why a waiting async task costs a small state object while a blocked thread costs a full stack
Trace how an async fn compiles to a state machine and predict its poll count and what it stores
Describe the waker contract and how Tokio's I/O driver turns epoll events into task wakeups
Compute how Tokio's work stealing, overflow and LIFO slot move tasks between queues
Diagnose blocking and starvation bugs and choose between spawn_blocking, coop budgets and dedicated threads

lessons.title: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap

blocks.md:
Recall the epoll event loop: one thread asks the kernel which sockets are ready, then services each ready socket without blocking. It is fast, but the code is inside out. Every connection's progress lives in hand-written state ("read the header, now waiting for the body") and every step is a callback.

The simple alternative is **one OS thread per connection**: write straight-line code, call blocking `read`, and let the kernel switch threads. That reads well but it pays for every waiting connection with a whole thread.

What does a waiting thread cost? Each thread needs its own stack. Rust's standard library currently gives spawned threads a **2 MiB** stack on all Tier-1 platforms ([std::thread](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/index.html)). Switching between threads also goes through the kernel scheduler, which you met as a context switch.

Now compare what a waiting connection actually *needs* to remember: its buffer, a few counters, and where it was in the code. For an echo handler that holds a 1 KiB buffer across its wait, that is about 1 KiB, not megabytes.

blocks.title: Memory set aside for N waiting connections

scenes.caption: At 10,000 connections, threads reserve 10,000 x 2 MiB = 20,000 MiB of stack, while 10,000 async tasks of 1,026 bytes each need about 9.78 MiB. The gap is a factor of about 2,044.

Shrinking stacks to 0.25 MiB helps, but threads still reserve 2,500 MiB at 10,000 connections. Simplified: a stack is reserved address space and only touched pages become resident, but the per-thread cost stays.
Even a fat 16 KiB task state stays far below one small thread stack. The task's size is set by what it holds across a wait, which you control.

blocks.md:
A **coroutine** is a function that can **suspend** in the middle and later **resume** where it left off. With coroutines you write straight-line code like the thread version, but a suspended coroutine is just a small saved object, and switching between coroutines is an ordinary function call and return inside your process.

Two designs exist:

- **Stackful** coroutines get their own stack, so they can suspend from any depth of nested calls, but each one still needs stack memory.
- **Stackless** coroutines suspend by *returning* to their caller and keep only the data needed to resume in a separate object. Both C++20 coroutines and Rust's `async fn` are stackless ([cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/coroutines)).

Coroutines alone do not do I/O. Someone must decide which suspended coroutine to resume next, and must learn from the kernel when a socket is ready. That someone is an **async runtime**. In Rust the language provides `async`/`await` and the `Future` trait, and libraries provide the runtime. The most widely used is **Tokio**, which bundles an I/O event loop (it calls this the *driver*), a scheduler that runs tasks, and a timer ([tokio::runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/runtime/index.html)).

scenes.caption: The compiler turns your async function into a Future value. Spawning it hands it to the runtime as a task.
The scheduler runs a task by calling its poll method. The task runs until it would have to wait, then returns.
Waiting tasks cost no thread. The I/O driver asks the kernel which sockets are ready, the epoll loop you already know.
When a socket a task waits on becomes ready, the driver wakes that task and the scheduler polls it again. Lessons 2 to 4 open up each arrow.

blocks.md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

blocks.question: A service has 20,000 open WebSocket connections that are idle 99% of the time, plus a CPU-heavy image resize per request. Which statement is right?
options: Async makes the image resize itself run faster because tasks switch without the kernel
Async lets idle connections cost a small state object each, but the resize still needs real CPU time and must not hog a runtime thread
Async only helps if every connection is busy all the time
Thread per connection and async use the same memory, since both store a stack per connection
blocks.explain: The win is for *waiting*. Idle connections become small suspended futures instead of 20,000 thread stacks. CPU work takes the same CPU time either way, and lesson 5 shows why long CPU work on a runtime thread hurts every other task.

blocks.question: What makes Rust's `async fn` a *stackless* coroutine?
options: It cannot call other functions
It runs on the caller's stack forever and never suspends
It suspends by returning to its caller, and the data needed to resume lives in a separate object
It is only allowed inside a runtime with one thread
blocks.explain: Stackless means no private stack: suspending is a return, and the locals that must survive the suspension are stored in a separate state object (the future). Stackful coroutines instead keep a whole stack per coroutine.

lessons.title: Futures: lazy state machines driven by poll

blocks.md:
Rust's coroutine type is the `Future` trait. It has one required method:

`fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>`

Calling `poll` asks the future to make as much progress as it can *without blocking*. It returns `Poll::Ready(value)` when finished or `Poll::Pending` when it must wait. Once a future has returned `Ready`, it should not be polled again ([std::future::Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/future/trait.Future.html)).

Two facts surprise people coming from other languages.

1. **Futures are lazy.** Calling an `async fn` runs none of its body. It just builds a future value. Nothing happens until someone polls it, usually via `.await` or by spawning it.
2. **The future is the computation itself**, not a handle to work happening in the background. As the Tokio tutorial puts it, the owner of the future is responsible for advancing it by calling `poll` ([Async in depth](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial/async)).

blocks.prompt: `let f = my_async_fn();` where the body starts with `println!("hello")`. Nothing else uses `f` and the function returns. What is printed?
blocks.reveal: Nothing. `my_async_fn()` only constructs the future. The `println!` runs on the first `poll`, and since `f` is dropped unpolled, the body never runs. The compiler warns that futures do nothing unless you `.await` or poll them.

blocks.md: How does a function become a value that can stop and restart? The compiler rewrites each `async fn` into a **state machine**: an enum with one variant per suspension point (each `.await`), where each variant holds the local variables that are still needed after that point. `poll` runs from the current state until it either finishes or reaches an `.await` whose child future returns `Pending`. Then it saves the state and returns. Below is the shape of that rewrite for a one-await function, following the Tokio tutorial's hand expansion.

blocks.title: Polling a compiled async fn twice

scenes.caption: The caller wrote `fetch()`. That only built the enum in state `Start`. No code from the body has run yet.
First poll. In `Start` the body runs up to the await: it creates the child future and moves into `Waiting`, storing the child inside itself.
The loop continues and polls the child. The socket has no data, so the child returns Pending. Fetch returns Pending too, keeping the child in its state.
Later the task is woken (lesson 3) and polled again. It resumes directly in `Waiting`: no stack had to be preserved, just this enum.
This time the child is ready with 512 bytes. Fetch moves to `Done` and returns Ready(512). A third poll would hit the panic arm.

blocks.md:
Notice that `Fetch` **contains** its child future. Futures nest: awaiting a future stores it inside the parent's state, so a whole call chain of async functions becomes one value whose size the compiler knows. When a task runs, the runtime polls the outermost future, which polls its child, and so on down to a leaf such as a socket read.

That is also why `poll` takes `Pin<&mut Self>`. A compiled state can hold a reference to one of its own fields (a borrow that lives across an `.await`). Moving the value would break that reference, so once polled, a future is *pinned* in place. The Tokio tutorial describes `Pin` as how Rust supports borrows in async functions ([std::pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/index.html)).

scenes.caption: A future that holds nothing across its await is 2 bytes. Holding a 1,024 byte buffer across the await makes it 1,026: the buffer must live in the state.
If the buffer is used and dropped *before* the await (inside a block), only a 1 byte result crosses the await, and the future is 3 bytes.
Two awaits: a 256 B array still in scope at the second await is stored next to the 512 B one (770 B). Scoping the 256 B array to end before the second await lets them share space: 514 B, 256 B less.

blocks.md: Sizes measured with `std::mem::size_of_val` on rustc 1.90; exact numbers can change between compiler versions. The rule that holds: a future stores what is **in scope across an await**. Big buffers that live across awaits make every task that holds them bigger, so box them or end their scope early.

C++20 coroutines take a similar stackless approach with different defaults. A function becomes a coroutine by using `co_await`, `co_yield` or `co_return`. Its *coroutine state* (parameters, locals that live across suspension, the current suspension point and a *promise* object) is allocated with `operator new` unless the compiler can optimize the allocation out. The promise's `initial_suspend` decides whether the body starts eagerly or lazily, and `co_await` calls an awaiter's `await_ready`, `await_suspend(handle)` and `await_resume`. `await_suspend` is responsible for arranging the resumption, for example by handing the handle to an I/O callback ([cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/coroutines)).

blocks.question: `async fn two() { yield_once().await; yield_once().await; }` where `yield_once()` returns Pending on its first poll (after waking itself) and Ready on its second. How many polls does the task need before `two` returns Ready?
blocks.explain: Poll 1 runs to the first await and gets Pending. Poll 2 resumes there, the first child is Ready, the body runs on to the second await and gets Pending. Poll 3 finishes. We confirmed this by polling such a future with a no-op waker: 2 Pending results, then Ready on poll 3.

blocks.question: A handler does `let mut buf = vec![0u8; 65536]; let n = sock.read(&mut buf).await?;` versus `let mut buf = [0u8; 65536];` with the same read. With 50,000 connections, which is the better choice for memory, and why?
options: The array, because stack memory is free in async code
Both are identical, since the compiler always boxes large locals
The array, because Vec allocations are not allowed across an await
The Vec: the future then stores only a pointer, length and capacity, while the array would make the future itself 64 KiB larger
blocks.explain: Anything in scope across an await lives inside the future. A 64 KiB array becomes part of every task's state machine (and is moved when the future is moved before pinning). A Vec stores its bytes on the heap, so the future only holds the small Vec header. Both still use the 64 KiB per connection; the Vec just keeps the future small and the buffer reusable.

lessons.title: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again

blocks.md:
A `Pending` result raises a question: when should the runtime poll this future again? Polling in a loop works but burns a CPU core. The Tokio tutorial's first "mini Tokio" does exactly that: it keeps a queue of tasks, pops one, polls it and pushes it back if `Pending`, forever.

The fix is the **waker**. Every call to `poll` receives a `Context`, and `cx.waker()` returns a `Waker` bound to the current task. Calling `wake()` on it tells the executor "poll this task again". The executor then only polls tasks that were woken.

The future contract: **if `poll` returns `Pending`, the future must make sure the waker from that call gets woken later** when progress is possible. Forget it and the task hangs forever, with no error. The Tokio tutorial calls this a common source of bugs.

For sockets, the thing that calls `wake()` is the runtime's **I/O driver**, which sits on top of epoll on Linux (through the mio crate). Here is the path of one `socket.read(&mut buf).await` in Tokio, simplified from its source:

1. The read checks the socket's cached readiness. If not readable, it stores the task's waker in the socket's registration and returns `Pending`.
2. When the worker has nothing else to run, the driver calls `epoll_wait`.
3. The kernel reports the socket readable. The driver sets the cached readiness and calls the stored waker, which puts the task back in a run queue.
4. The scheduler polls the task. The read runs `read(2)` and gets bytes.

blocks.title: One socket read: Pending, wake, Ready

scenes.caption: The worker polls the task. Inside, the read finds the socket not readable, stores the waker in the socket's registration and returns Pending. No system call blocked.
With no runnable tasks left, the worker drives the I/O driver, which sleeps in epoll_wait until some registered socket changes state.
Data arrives. epoll reports the socket readable; the driver records the readiness and calls waker.wake(), which queues the task.
The worker polls the task again. The read now calls read(2), gets the bytes and returns Ready. The task runs on to its next await.

blocks.md:
Two details make this robust.

- **The waker can change.** A future may move to a different task between polls (for example, polled once and then spawned). Only the waker from the *most recent* `poll` must be woken, so a future that stores a waker must replace it when `!stored.will_wake(cx.waker())`.
- **Spurious wakeups are allowed.** A task may be polled when nothing changed, and Tokio's docs say it may schedule tasks that were not woken. A future must simply check again and return `Pending` if still not ready. Tokio's socket read does this: if `read(2)` returns `WouldBlock`, it clears the cached readiness and loops back to wait.

blocks.prompt: A future checks `if !ready.load() { store(cx.waker().clone()); return Pending }`. The event source sets `ready = true` and then wakes whatever waker is stored. What can go wrong?
blocks.reveal:
A **lost wakeup**. If the event fires *between* the check and the store, the source wakes the old waker (or none), and then the future stores its waker and returns `Pending`. Nobody will ever wake it.

The standard fix is to check again *after* storing the waker. Tokio's `ScheduledIo::poll_readiness` does exactly this: after storing the waker under the waiters lock it re-reads the readiness "in case the readiness was changed while we were taking the waiters lock".

blocks.caption: A busy-polling block_on. It works but spins; replacing the noop waker with one that unparks this thread is what turns it into a real executor.

blocks.question: A custom timer future, when not yet expired, returns `Poll::Pending` without storing or using `cx.waker()`, assuming the runtime will poll it again soon. On Tokio, what happens?
options: It works: Tokio re-polls every pending task every tick
It panics with "polled after completion"
The task may never be polled again and hangs silently unless something else happens to wake it
Tokio detects the missing waker and converts it into a busy loop
blocks.explain: Executors only re-poll tasks that are woken (spurious wakeups are possible but never guaranteed). Returning Pending without arranging a wake breaks the Future contract and the task can sleep forever.

blocks.question: A `Delay` future is polled once in task X, then moved into a new task Y and polled there. Which waker must it wake when the time expires?
options: Both X's and Y's wakers, to be safe
Y's waker, from the most recent poll
X's waker, from the first poll
Neither: wakers are per runtime, not per task
blocks.explain: The Future docs say only the waker from the most recent poll should be scheduled. The Tokio tutorial's fixed Delay compares the stored waker with `will_wake` on every poll and replaces it if the task changed. Waking X would poll the wrong task, and Y would hang.

lessons.title: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot

blocks.md:
A Tokio **task** is a spawned top-level future plus bookkeeping, and the docs call tasks green threads: scheduled by the runtime instead of the OS, so switching between them needs no kernel context switch ([tokio::task](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/index.html)). Tokio offers two schedulers:

- **Current-thread**: all tasks run on the one thread that calls `block_on`.
- **Multi-thread** (the default): a pool of worker threads, by default one per CPU core, using **work stealing**.

Why not one shared queue for all workers? Every push and pop would contend on it. Tokio's 2019 scheduler rewrite ([Making the Tokio scheduler 10x faster](https://tokio.rs/blog/2019-10-scheduler)) instead gives each worker its own **local queue** and adds a shared **global queue**. The runtime docs describe today's multi-thread behavior (and warn it may change):

- A local queue holds at most **256** tasks. If it overflows, half of them move to the global queue.
- A worker takes from its local queue first, and checks the global queue when the local one is empty or after picking local tasks `global_queue_interval` times in a row (if not set, tuned at runtime to aim for about 10 ms between checks).
- With both empty, a worker **steals half** of another worker's local queue.
- It checks for I/O and timer events when nothing is runnable, or after **61** tasks in a row (`event_interval`).

scenes.caption: Each worker thread runs tasks from its own local queue. Most pushes and pops touch only that queue, so workers rarely contend.
A task woken on a worker thread (here by the driver run on worker 0) goes into that worker's own run queue. A task woken from a thread outside the runtime goes to the global queue.
Worker 0 is flooded. When its local queue would exceed 256 tasks, half of them move to the global queue, where any worker can pick them up.
Worker 1 ran dry. It checks the global queue, and if that is empty too, steals half of worker 0's local queue. Idle cores pull work to themselves.

blocks.title: Steal, LIFO slot and overflow, step by step

scenes.caption: Simplified: queues drawn with 8 slots instead of 256. Worker 0 has 5 queued tasks. Worker 1's local queue and the global queue are empty, so worker 1 goes stealing.
Worker 1 takes n minus n/2 (rounded down) = 5 minus 2 = 3 tasks from the head: T1, T2, T3. Worker 0 keeps T4 and T5. Both cores now have work.
Worker 0 runs T4, which sends a message that wakes T6. A task woken by a running task goes into the LIFO slot, not the back of the queue.
When T4 yields, worker 0 runs T6 immediately, ahead of T5. The receiver handles the message while it is still hot in cache. Other workers cannot steal from the LIFO slot.
Later, worker 0's local queue is full (8 here, 256 in Tokio) and T14 must be queued.
Overflow: the newer half (T10 to T13) plus T14 move to the global queue in one batch. In Tokio that is 128 tasks plus the new one. Worker 0 keeps the older half.

blocks.tex: \text{stolen} = n - \left\lfloor n/2 \right\rfloor = \left\lceil n/2 \right\rceil, \qquad \text{overflow moved} = 256/2 = 128 \;(+1\text{ new task})
blocks.caption: From Tokio's queue.rs: a stealer claims the larger half of the victim's queued tasks; an overflowing worker moves the newer half plus the task being pushed.

blocks.md: The **LIFO slot** fixes a latency problem of plain FIFO queues. In a message-passing pattern, task A sends to task B and then waits. With FIFO, B goes to the back of a possibly long queue even though its data is hot in cache. Tokio runs B next instead. To stop two tasks ping-ponging forever, a worker uses the LIFO slot at most **3** times in a row, and the coop budget (lesson 5) is not reset for LIFO polls. The current-thread scheduler has no LIFO slot; it checks the global queue every **31** local picks by default.

Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`.

blocks.question: Worker 2 finds its local queue and the global queue empty, while worker 0's local queue holds 9 tasks. How many tasks does worker 2 take in one steal, and from which end?
options: 4, from the newest end
1, the oldest task
9, all of them
5, from the head (the oldest tasks)
blocks.explain: The stealer claims n minus floor(n/2) = 9 minus 4 = 5 tasks, starting at the head of the victim's queue, which is also where the owner pops. Taking half at once means the thief does not have to come back for every task.

blocks.question: Why does Tokio use per-worker local queues plus stealing instead of a single shared run queue?
options: A shared queue cannot hold more than 256 tasks
Most pushes and pops then touch only the worker's own queue, avoiding contention on one shared structure, while stealing still balances load
Stealing guarantees strict FIFO order across the whole runtime
Local queues let the OS preempt long-running tasks
blocks.explain: A single queue is simple but every worker contends on it. Sharding into local queues removes most contention; work stealing (and the global queue for overflow and outside wakeups) keeps idle workers busy. Ordering becomes looser, which Tokio's docs say explicitly.

lessons.title: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation

blocks.md:
Tokio tasks are **cooperatively** scheduled: a task runs until its `poll` returns, which happens only at an `.await` that is not ready. The OS can preempt a *thread*, but Tokio cannot preempt a *task*. Rust's async state machines give an executor no way to inject yield points, as the Tokio team explains in its [preemption post](https://tokio.rs/blog/2020-04-preemption).

So anything that holds a worker thread without reaching a pending `.await` stalls every other task waiting for that thread. Two common culprits: **blocking calls** such as `std::thread::sleep`, synchronous file or database APIs, or a blocking mutex held for long; and **long CPU work** such as hashing a big file or parsing a huge JSON body.

blocks.title: One blocking call on a current-thread runtime

scenes.caption: Model: B and C have timers that expire at 10 ms and 20 ms and need 1 ms of work each. A calls std::thread::sleep(50 ms) and holds the only thread from 0 to 50 ms.
B's timer fired at 10 ms and C's at 20 ms, but nobody could poll them. They run at 50 to 51 and 51 to 52 ms: 40 ms and 31 ms late.
With tokio::time::sleep(50 ms).await, A returns Pending and frees the thread. B runs at 10 to 11 ms and C at 20 to 21 ms, right on time; A still finishes at 50 ms.

blocks.md: How long is too long? Alice Ryhl, a Tokio maintainer, gives a rule of thumb of **no more than 10 to 100 microseconds between `.await`s**, depending on the application ([Async: What is blocking?](https://ryhl.io/blog/async-what-is-blocking/)). Ryhl also notes the trap: on a multi-thread runtime with about 8 cores, a few blocking tasks go unnoticed in local tests and then exhaust every worker under real load.

The opposite failure exists too: a task that is **never** pending. Under load, an echo loop's socket may always have more data, so `read().await` is always ready and the task never yields. Since Tokio 0.2.14 every task gets an operation **budget of 128** per scheduling. Each Tokio resource operation (socket, timer, channel) spends one unit. At zero, Tokio resources pretend to be not ready, forcing the task to yield; the budget resets when it is next scheduled. The Tokio post reports tail latencies dropping by almost 3x in some cases.

blocks.title: Messages task A took before task B first ran

scenes.caption: Measured on Tokio 1.53, current-thread runtime: A drains a channel holding 1,000 ready messages, B is waiting. With the budget, A is forced to yield after 128 receives and B runs.
Wrapped in unconstrained, A's receives never run out of budget, so A consumed all 1,000 messages before B ran once. Draining 1,000 messages with the budget takes 8 turns (7 x 128 + 104).

blocks.md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

Tools for work that cannot avoid blocking:

- `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(closure)` runs a closure on a separate **blocking pool** and returns a handle you can `.await`. Threads are added on demand up to `max_blocking_threads`, **512** by default, and exit after **10 seconds** idle. Even a current-thread runtime uses this pool.
- Because that limit is large, the docs advise limiting CPU-bound work (for example with a semaphore) or using a CPU pool such as rayon.
- For work that runs indefinitely, use a dedicated `std::thread::spawn` thread instead of occupying a pool thread ([spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html)).

blocks.caption: spawn_blocking turns blocking work into something the async task can await. hash_file_sync stands for any synchronous function.

blocks.md: Cooperative scheduling also defines **cancellation**. Dropping a future, or calling `JoinHandle::abort` on a task, stops it at the `.await` where it is suspended and runs the destructors of its live locals; it never resumes. That is cheap and clean, but any code after that await simply does not run, so a step like "write the record, then update the index" split across two awaits can be cut in half. A `spawn_blocking` closure that has started cannot be aborted at all, because it has no await points.

blocks.question: A Tokio service on 8 cores calls a synchronous database driver directly in each request handler. Load tests with 4 concurrent requests look fine; production with 200 concurrent requests shows multi-second latency spikes even for /health. What is the best fix?
options: Raise event_interval so the I/O driver runs more often
Run the driver calls in spawn_blocking (or use an async driver) so worker threads keep polling other tasks
Switch to the current-thread runtime to avoid stealing overhead
Call tokio::task::yield_now() before each query
blocks.explain: Each blocking query pins a worker. With 8 workers, 8 slow queries freeze every other task, including /health. Moving blocking calls to the blocking pool (or an async client) frees the workers. yield_now before the query does not help because the blocking happens after it.

blocks.question: You wrap a CPU-heavy image resize in spawn_blocking and spawn 2,000 of them at once on an 8-core machine. What is the main risk?
options: Tokio rejects spawn_blocking calls beyond the number of cores
The resizes run on the async worker threads and block I/O
Up to 512 blocking threads compete for 8 cores, adding memory and switching overhead; a semaphore or a CPU pool like rayon bounds parallelism
spawn_blocking tasks are aborted after 10 seconds
blocks.explain: The blocking pool grows to max_blocking_threads (512 by default) and queues the rest. That suits blocking I/O but oversubscribes the CPU for compute. The 10 second figure is the idle timeout for pool threads, not a task deadline.

blocks.md: Async Rust in one breath: `async fn` compiles to a lazy state machine; `poll` advances it until an await is Pending; the waker plus the epoll-based driver decide when to poll again; Tokio's workers spread tasks with local queues and stealing; and because nothing preempts a task, every task must reach a Pending await often, or move blocking work to `spawn_blocking`.
